design_detail: Laboratory analytical-performance study of one fentanyl test strip product across five manufacturing lots, on drug standards dissolved in water rather than on drug samples or people. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are prepared solutions, and QUADAS-2 is used for appraisal, as for sc_green_2020, because strip readings are compared with known content. One laboratory (Department of Laboratory Medicine, ZSFG Clinical Laboratory, University of California San Francisco). Strips: BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strips with a 20 ng/mL urine cut-off (part FLY-1S48-100), a competitive lateral flow immunoassay; lots 082 and 004 obtained and tested in 2017, lots 018, 188 and 196 obtained in 2021 and tested in summer 2022 (lot 196 was the lot community advocates had reported as defective). Experiments: (1) lowest concentration read positive for fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and the non-fentanyl opioid U-47700 spiked into water at nine concentrations from 10 µg/mL to 10 ng/mL, in duplicate on every lot; (2) cross-reactivity of 11 other drugs and cutting agents at concentrations up to 150 mg/mL where enough standard was available; (3) fentanyl in drug-free urine versus water on the three 2021 lots (1 µg/mL to 20 ng/mL, duplicate). Strips were read by eye by two people and recorded by consensus. No drug samples were tested, so no sensitivity or specificity can be calculated.
can_establish: The lowest concentrations at which five lots of one fentanyl test strip product, obtained in 2017 or 2021, read positive for fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and U-47700 dissolved in water, and the concentrations at which pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine solutions gave false positives, in one laboratory.
cannot_establish: How often the strips are right with real drug samples (none were tested), whether the fall in fentanyl sensitivity between the 2017 and 2021 lots comes from manufacturing rather than from the separate testing rounds (2017 and 2022) or from storage, how mixtures, untested analogues, nitazenes or other cutting agents behave, how people prepare and read strips at home, or whether strip use changes behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Solutions, not people or seized samples: analytical standards bought from Cayman Chemicals or Cerilliant, diluted in analytical-grade water (Fisher Scientific) or drug-free human urine (Golden West Diagnostics) (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph). The number of strips used is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Opioids: fentanyl, the 13 most cited fentanyl analogues in the authors' description (the 11 that cross-reacted plus sufentanil and alfentanil) and U-47700 (Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). Interference panel (editors' count, 11 as the authors state): heroin, 6-acetylcodeine, quinidine, cocaine, ketamine, diphenhydramine, lidocaine, MDMA, l- and d-methamphetamine, levamisole. Upper concentrations were limited to 10, 25 or 50 mg/mL for some substances by the amount of standard that could be bought (Methods › Interferences).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. No invalid strips are reported except several lot-196 strips with no control line at 50 mg/mL diphenhydramine (marked N/A in Fig. 2). No result for a drug-free water blank is reported.
sample.selection_effects: Every solution held one pure analyte at a chosen concentration, so the design is two-gate by construction (known positives, known negatives) and lacks the matrix of real samples: mixtures, several cutting agents together, undissolved powder, pills or residues. The 2017 and 2021 lots were tested in separate rounds (2017 and summer 2022), and the strips were donated through DanceSafe, the organization that had published the community warning about lot performance (reference 49), and by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation, with storage and expiry not reported (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph; Funding).

exposure.measurement: Index test (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph): each strip immersed up to the maximum mark in the test solution for 10 s, laid flat on a clean surface, photographed and interpreted according to the maker's instructions within 5 min by two people independently, the result being recorded by consensus after discussion. The reading rule (which line pattern counts as positive, how faint lines were called) is not stated, nor how discordant duplicates were combined into a limit of detection. Blinding of readers to analyte and concentration is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (solutions). Study concentrations: opioids at 10 µg/mL, 5 µg/mL, 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 10 ng/mL in water; interferents up to 150 mg/mL where available; urine-water comparison at 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50 and 20 ng/mL. The authors equate the opioid range to 0.5% down to 0.0005% fentanyl by weight in an assumed 2 mg/mL drug solution (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable: each solution contained a single analyte; no mixture of fentanyl with an interfering substance, and no real drug sample, was tested.

comparison.controls: Reference: the known concentration of purchased analytical standards spiked into water or drug-free urine; prepared concentrations were not verified analytically (for example by LC-MS). Whether the standards were solids or solvent solutions, and the solvent content of the test solutions, are not reported. On-label comparison: fentanyl in drug-free urine on the three 2021 lots, tested alongside water.
comparison.matching: Both rounds were run in the same laboratory space with the principal investigator present to keep methods continuous (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph); whether the readers, standard batches and water were the same in both rounds is not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to solutions. Not measured or not reported: strip storage, expiry dates and age at testing; any side-by-side test of a 2017 lot and a 2021 lot in the same round; individual reader calls (only consensus was kept); the rule for faint lines; how duplicates were combined; the concentrations tested for each interferent (Fig. 2, image).

outcomes.instruments: Lowest concentration read positive (limit of detection) for each opioid and lot; lowest concentration of each other substance that read positive (false-positive threshold) for each lot; limit of detection for fentanyl in urine versus water. Per-lot values are shown in Figs. 1–2 and Additional file 2 (images).
outcomes.validity_norms: The maker's 20 ng/mL cut-off is defined for urine, and the authors show that water and urine differ (Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison). The concentration steps were two- to fivefold apart (for example 200, 100, 50, 20 ng/mL), so each limit is known only to within one step.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = strip read positive by the consensus of two readers at a given concentration; a limit of detection is the lowest step read positive for an opioid, a false-positive threshold the lowest step read positive for a non-target substance. No sensitivity, specificity or predictive values.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no statistical tests or intervals).

analysis.effect_sizes: No accuracy statistics and no sample-level counts are given, so the editors could not count true and false results or compute intervals. Text values: fentanyl in water detected down to 20 ng/mL with the 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL with the 2021 lots; in urine, 50 ng/mL (lots 018 and 196) and 100 ng/mL (the third 2021 lot). False-positive thresholds, 2017 lots: d-methamphetamine 5, MDMA 50, diphenhydramine and lidocaine 100 mg/mL; 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 10, MDMA 2.5–5, lidocaine 2.5, diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL. Editors' calculation of the change from the 2017 to the 2021 lots: fentanyl limit 10-fold higher; thresholds 10- to 20-fold lower for MDMA, 40-fold lower for lidocaine, 100- to 200-fold lower for diphenhydramine and 2-fold higher for d-methamphetamine.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five lots are reported for the opioids; the 2021 lots were tested only with substances already known to interfere plus levamisole, and only the 2021 lots were tested in urine. Per-lot values for analogues and interferents are given only as figure images. Additional file 3 (Table S1 A–D: estimated strip results for methamphetamine and MDMA samples with and without trace fentanyl at different solution concentrations) is a DOCX download and was not read.
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning. Duplicate strips per step, consensus reading and no repeatability estimate mean that one-step differences between lots cannot be told apart from test-to-test variation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In water, two lots obtained in 2017 (tested in 2017) detected fentanyl at 20 ng/mL and three lots obtained in 2021 (tested in 2022) only at 200 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also fell short of the maker's 20 ng/mL cut-off in urine (50–100 ng/mL). All lots detected 11 fentanyl analogues; none detected alfentanil or U-47700, and the 2021 lots missed sufentanil. Pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine gave false positives at mg/mL concentrations, at lower concentrations with the 2021 lots except for d-methamphetamine; heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were shown negative only up to 10 µg/mL.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports “notable lot-to-lot variability in the sensitivity of the strips for fentanyl” (Abstract › Results), but within each testing round the fentanyl limit was the same for every lot; the tenfold difference lies between strips obtained in 2017 and in 2021 and tested in separate rounds, so lot, storage and round cannot be separated, and the Conclusion's call for distributors to disclose manufacturing changes points to a manufacturing cause that the design cannot establish. The Discussion presents the fall as matching other laboratory results of the period (1st paragraph), but Table 1 gives publication years, not testing years or lots, and limits of 25–200 ng/mL in no time order. It argues that community guidance to dilute stimulant samples to 2 mg/mL now leaves strips open to MDMA false positives (3rd paragraph), although the lowest MDMA concentration that gave a false positive was 2.5 mg/mL (whether 2 mg/mL itself was tested is shown only in Fig. 2, an image); for diphenhydramine, whose thresholds (0.5–1 mg/mL) lie below 2 mg/mL, the argument holds. The abstract's statement that the strips remain an important overdose prevention tool is not tested here.

timeline.event: Lots 082 and 004 obtained and tested (this study's first round).
Green et al. (2020): strip limit of detection 100 ng/mL, 2 of 2 analogues cross-reacted (as summarized in this paper's Table 1).
McCrae et al. (2020), British Columbia drug checking: strips missed fentanyl in 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples, all at 5% fentanyl by weight or less; cited in the Discussion, not read.
Bergh et al. (2021): limit 50 ng/mL, 25 of 28 analogues cross-reacted, no interference among the substances assessed; Wharton et al. (2021): limit 100 ng/mL, 19 of 29 analogues (Table 1); not read.
Lockwood et al. (2021): limit 25 ng/mL; false positives with methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine (Table 1); read for this batch (card sc_lockwood_2021).
Community notice (DanceSafe, 2021) that a recent batch of strips required different dilutions; lot 196 was the lot reported as defective (Background, 7th paragraph; reference 49); not read.
Park et al. (2022): limit 200 ng/mL, 13 of 17 analogues (Table 1); not read. Lots 018, 188 and 196 tested in summer 2022 (this study's second round).

De Vrieze et al. (2024) cite this study for fentanyl strip lots with limits up to ten times the maker's cut-off and ask for the same lot transparency for nitazene strips; read for this batch (card sc_de_vrieze_2024).

replication.where_it_stands: Fentanyl limits for this strip type range from 25 to 200 ng/mL across the independent evaluations in Table 1, which fits lot or method variation, but no paper read here tested old and new lots side by side in one round. False positives from methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine appear both here, with pure standards, and in Lockwood et al. (2021), with seized and retail material, at thresholds that differ by lot and method; among the papers read, lidocaine interference with fentanyl strips and the stereospecificity for d-methamphetamine are reported only here.

funding.funder: No specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (Funding). The competing-interest statement adds that D.C.'s effort was supported by NIH/NIDA grants DA037820 and DA054190. Strips were donated: all lots except DOA2101018 by Emanuel Sferios in partnership with DanceSafe, a peer-based not-for-profit harm-reduction organization; lot DOA2101018 by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation (Funding; Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: J.H., L.L. and K.L. declare nothing to disclose. D.C. is a scientific advisor to Celero Systems and is retained as an expert by Motley-Rice LLC in ongoing opioid litigation (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the UCSF Department of Laboratory Medicine (ZSFG Clinical Laboratory) and Department of Family and Community Medicine. The strips came through DanceSafe, which had published the warning about lot performance, with Emanuel Sferios, who is thanked for his advocacy on lot-to-lot variability, the question tested here, and from the San Francisco AIDS Foundation; no support from the strip maker is mentioned. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Several current and earlier lots tested side by side in one round with the same analytically verified standards, replicate strips and readers blinded to lot and concentration (with a repeatability estimate), strip age and storage recorded; and, for real-world accuracy, a blinded consecutive series of drug-checking samples, including stimulant samples and mixtures, tested on several lots against a quantitative reference such as LC-MS/MS.

domains.note: Artificial two-gate design: single pure analytes at chosen concentrations as positives and chosen non-target substances as negatives, with no real samples. Applicability to drug checking is low: no mixtures, combined cutting agents, residues or pills.

Two readers and photographs, but only consensus calls were kept; the rule for faint lines and the handling of discordant duplicates are not stated; reader blinding is not reported; high-concentration diphenhydramine strips with faint control lines were read as negative.
Known concentrations of purchased analytical standards, a sound reference for presence and amount, although the prepared concentrations were not verified analytically.

The 2017 and 2021 lots were tested in separate rounds (2017 and summer 2022) with separately prepared solutions and unreported strip storage and age, and not all lots met the same panel: the 2021 lots were tested only with known interferents plus levamisole, and only they were tested in urine.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because the study compares strip readings with known content (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domains: an artificial two-gate design and a lot comparison confounded with testing round. Within a round, the limits are credible laboratory values for pure analytes in water. Citable for: lots of this strip obtained in 2021 detected fentanyl in water at 200 ng/mL and in urine at 50–100 ng/mL, against 20 ng/mL in water for lots obtained in 2017 (tested in 2017 and 2022 respectively); all lots detected 11 fentanyl analogues, none detected alfentanil or U-47700; pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine gave false positives at the stated mg/mL concentrations, with thresholds that differed between lots. Not citable for: accuracy with real samples, a manufacturing cause of the change, heroin or other untested substances not interfering at realistic concentrations, or effects on behaviour or overdose.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Not applicable: no organisms; the units are drug standards dissolved in water or drug-free urine.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Study conditions only: opioid standards at nine concentrations from 10 µg/mL to 10 ng/mL; interferents up to 150 mg/mL where available (some limited to 10, 25 or 50 mg/mL); duplicate strips; one 10-s immersion; reading within 5 min.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Partly. The strips are the most widely available brand and were used per the maker's instructions, but laboratory staff tested pure single analytes in analytical-grade water; drug checking as described in the Background dissolves drug in water as prepared for injection, rehydrates residues or dissolves a portion of a sample, at concentrations that are unknown and vary (Background, 5th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Five lots of BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strips with a 20 ng/mL urine cut-off (lots D607082, 16120004, DOA2101018, DOA2111188 and DOA2105196, called 082, 004, 018, 188 and 196) were tested in one laboratory: lots 082 and 004 were obtained and evaluated in 2017, lots 018, 188 and 196 obtained in 2021 and evaluated in summer 2022, in the same laboratory space with the principal investigator present at both rounds. Lot 196 was the lot community advocates had reported as defective.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph; Background, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and U-47700 were spiked into water at 10 µg/mL, 5 µg/mL, 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 10 ng/mL and tested in duplicate on each lot. Each strip was immersed to the maximum mark for 10 s, laid flat, photographed and read within 5 min by two people independently, with the result recorded by consensus. The authors equate these concentrations to 0.5% down to 0.0005% fentanyl by weight in an assumed 2 mg/mL drug solution.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl in water: the two 2017 lots read positive down to 20 ng/mL, the maker's urine cut-off; the three 2021 lots only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher. Editors' calculation at the authors' assumed 2 mg/mL solution: 0.001% and 0.01% fentanyl by weight.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (image)
key_findings.note: Lot and testing round coincide: the 2017 lots were tested in 2017 and the 2021 lots in 2022.

key_findings.finding: All five lots cross-reacted with 11 fentanyl analogues: 3-methylfentanyl, acetyl fentanyl, acrylfentanyl, β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl, butyrylfentanyl, carfentanil, cyclopropylfentanyl, fluorobutyrylfentanyl, furanyl fentanyl, p-fluorofentanyl and tetrahydrofuran fentanyl. The 2017 lots also detected sufentanil and the 2021 lots did not; no lot detected alfentanil or U-47700 at any concentration tested (highest 10 µg/mL).
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph; Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Analogue limits by lot: compared with the 2017 lots, the 2021 lots had limits 10 to 50 times lower for acetyl fentanyl, β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl, furanyl fentanyl and p-fluorofentanyl, and poorer sensitivity for acrylfentanyl (except lot 196), butyrylfentanyl and carfentanil (lot 018 better than the other 2021 lots but worse than the 2017 lots); 3-methylfentanyl, fluorobutyrylfentanyl and tetrahydrofuran fentanyl were about the same in all lots. The two 2017 lots did not differ; among the 2021 lots, analogue limits often differed by one to two dilution steps, most for acrylfentanyl, carfentanil and cyclopropylfentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Per-lot limits for each analogue are shown only in Fig. 1, an image; values were not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Interference, 2017 lots: no cross-reactivity with heroin, 6-acetylcodeine or quinidine at 10 µg/mL, or with cocaine or ketamine at 25 mg/mL; false positives with diphenhydramine and lidocaine at 100 mg/mL, MDMA at 50 mg/mL and d-methamphetamine at 5 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine was negative at 25 mg/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were tested only up to 10 µg/mL as printed, 200 times below the 2 mg/mL solution the authors assume (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Interference, 2021 lots (tested with substances already known to interfere, plus levamisole): lidocaine gave false positives at 2.5 mg/mL and d-methamphetamine at 10 mg/mL in all three lots; MDMA at 5 mg/mL (lots 018 and 188) and 2.5 mg/mL (lot 196); diphenhydramine at 0.5 mg/mL (lots 018 and 188) and 1 mg/mL (lot 196); levamisole showed no cross-reactivity up to 100 mg/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 (image)

key_findings.finding: With the 2021 lots, diphenhydramine at 50 and 100 mg/mL gave unusually faint control lines and extremely faint to invisible test lines, which the readers agreed to call negative; repeating the experiments gave the same result, and several lot-196 strips showed no control line at 50 mg/mL (invalid). The authors call these results paradoxical and unexplained.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the reported thresholds, 2017 to 2021 lots: the fentanyl limit rose 10-fold; the false-positive threshold fell 10- to 20-fold for MDMA, 40-fold for lidocaine and 100- to 200-fold for diphenhydramine, and rose 2-fold for d-methamphetamine. The Conclusion describes the change for diphenhydramine, lidocaine and MDMA as a 10-to-100-fold increase in sensitivity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl in drug-free urine (the on-label matrix), three 2021 lots: positive down to 50 ng/mL (lots 018 and 196) and 100 ng/mL (the third lot, printed 118), better than in water tested at the same time (which reproduced the 200 ng/mL limit) but above the maker's 20 ng/mL urine cut-off; lines were visibly brighter in urine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison, 1st paragraph; Methods › Urine and water eluent comparison, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The per-lot results are in Additional file 2 (Fig. S2, a TIFF download), not read.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 summarizes five earlier independent evaluations of the same strip (publication year, fentanyl limit in ng/mL): Green et al. 2020, 100; Bergh et al. 2021, 50; Lockwood et al. 2021, 25; Wharton et al. 2021, 100; Park et al. 2022, 200. Analogue cross-reactivity: 2 of 2, 25 of 28, not assessed, 19 of 29 and 13 of 17 assessed; interferences were assessed only by Bergh et al. (none found) and Lockwood et al. (methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (separate HTML table page); Background, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion cites British Columbia drug-checking data (McCrae et al., 2020) in which the strips missed fentanyl in 4 of 173 (2.3%) fentanyl-positive samples confirmed by qNMR, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less, using sample solutions of about 30 µg/mL; 70% of those samples were expected to be opioids and 9% stimulants.

The maker claims a 20 ng/mL cut-off for fentanyl and norfentanyl in urine and detection of ten named analogues; three of them (remifentanil, ocfentanil, valeryl fentanyl) were not tested here, and the 2021 lots did not detect a fourth (sufentanil).
key_findings.locator: Background, 5th paragraph; Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: only 13 fentanyl analogues and 11 other drugs and adulterants were tested; reading line presence by eye is subjective; only consensus decisions were recorded, so agreement between readers (kappa) cannot be calculated; not all strip results are clearly positive or negative.

The authors conclude that the strips remain useful as part of an overdose-prevention cascade that should include more sophisticated drug checking, and call for independent assessment of each lot and for distributors to disclose changes in reagents and manufacturing.

reporting_issues.issue: In the urine comparison the Results name the third 2021 lot 118; no lot 118 was tested (the 2021 lots are 018, 188 and 196) (Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 100 ng/mL urine limit presumably belongs to lot 188.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion summarizes the 2017-to-2021 change in false-positive thresholds for diphenhydramine, lidocaine and MDMA as 10-to-100-fold; the thresholds in the Results give 10- to 20-fold (MDMA), 40-fold (lidocaine) and 100- to 200-fold (diphenhydramine) (editors' calculation) (Conclusion, 2nd paragraph; Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the thresholds, not the summary range.

reporting_issues.issue: Heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were tested only up to 10 µg/mL as printed (Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st paragraph), although the Methods say high upper concentrations (150 mg/mL where available) were chosen, and the substances that interfered did so only from 0.5 mg/mL upward.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a misprint or a much lower ceiling; either way the paper cannot be cited for heroin not causing false positives at the mg/mL concentrations of drug checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports notable lot-to-lot variability in fentanyl sensitivity, but within each round every lot had the same fentanyl limit (20 ng/mL for both 2017 lots, 200 ng/mL for all three 2021 lots); the difference lies between lots obtained in different years and tested in different rounds (Abstract › Results; Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe a difference between lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 and tested in 2017 and 2022, not variation between lots of one period.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the strips were obtained from BTNX, while the Funding statement says all lots except DOA2101018 were provided by DanceSafe and lot DOA2101018 by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation; storage conditions, expiry dates and time from receipt to testing are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Deterioration in storage cannot be separated from manufacturing differences, which matters most for the 2021 lots, obtained in 2021 and tested in 2022.

reporting_issues.issue: The Funding statement says the work received no specific grant, while the competing-interest statement says one author's effort was supported by two NIH/NIDA grants (DA037820, DA054190).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both are recorded under funding.

reporting_issues.issue: Testing was in duplicate, but the rule for combining discordant duplicates into a limit, the rule for faint lines and the individual reader calls are not reported (only consensus was kept), and no drug-free water blank result is given (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Differences of one dilution step between lots may lie within test-to-test variation, which was not measured.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12954-023-00921-8 (Harm Reduction Journal 21, article 14, 2024; version of record 18 January 2024), reached from https://doi.org/10.1186/s12954-023-00921-8: all text from Abstract to Conclusion; Table 1 (read on its separate HTML table page); legends of Figs. 1–2 (the figures are images; values not extracted beyond what the text states); data-availability, acknowledgement, funding, author-contribution, ethics and competing-interest statements; reference list; descriptions of Additional files 1–3. The additional files (two TIFF figures and a DOCX table) are downloads and were not read. No print pagination; anchors give publisher HTML with section and paragraph.

The instrument (QUADAS-2) and every judgment are unchanged.
